name: Retro Console
basis: early 3D console artifacts: vertex snapping, affine textures, dithered colour depth, fog (how)

lumenary.blurb: A frame from an early 3D games console: a few hundred lines of picture, a small colour depth held together by dithering, textures that swim across wobbling polygons, and fog in the distance.

facts.bestOn: Scenes with depth: streets, rooms, landscapes

why: Early 3D consoles had to draw a world thirty times a second on very little hardware, and every shortcut left a mark. Polygon corners snapped to whole pixels, so surfaces wobbled. Textures were stretched without perspective, so they swam. Colour was stored in few bits and dithered. Distance was hidden in fog. Together those faults are a look that a generation remembers.
how: Shrink the picture to a few hundred lines.
Lay a mesh over it, nudge every corner and round it to a whole pixel.
Inside each triangle, read the picture at a straight blend of its three corners, with no perspective.
Fade the upper part of the frame toward a fog colour taken from the picture.
Cut the colour to a small depth, deciding ties with a 4 by 4 Bayer pattern.
Enlarge without smoothing and darken part of every line.
history: Home consoles moved to 3D in the mid 1990s: the Sega Saturn and the first Sony PlayStation in 1994, the Nintendo 64 in 1996. The PlayStation worked with whole-pixel vertex positions and textures mapped without perspective correction, which gave its games their famous shimmer, and it dithered its 15-bit colour. Around 2015 independent developers began to copy those limits on purpose, and the “low-poly retro” look became a style in its own right.
uses: Game jam art and retro game mock-ups
terms: Stretching a texture across a triangle in straight proportion, ignoring perspective.
Mixing two shades in a fixed pattern to suggest the shades between them.
paragraphs: The picture is shrunk until its longer side has the chosen number of lines, and a mesh of squares about one eleventh of the frame high is laid over it. Every corner of the mesh is nudged by a random amount and then rounded to a whole pixel, which is what early consoles did to the corners of their polygons. Each square is split into two triangles, and inside a triangle the place the texture is read from is a straight blend of its three corners. That blend ignores perspective, so the picture kinks along the diagonal of every square and seems to swim. Each triangle is also lit as one flat face, a few percent lighter or darker than its neighbour.

Distance is faked by height in the frame: the upper part fades toward a fog colour taken from the average of the top third of the picture. Finally the colour is cut to the chosen depth, 32, 8 or 4 levels a channel. A value between two levels is rounded up or down by comparing its remainder with a 4 by 4 Bayer matrix, so a smooth gradient becomes a regular weave of two neighbouring shades instead of a band. Scan lines darken the lower part of every picture line, and the game display is drawn into the small frame so that its pixels match the picture’s.

equations.note: Where a pixel reads the texture: s and t are its position inside the square, v the nudged and rounded corners. The other triangle uses the three remaining corners the same way.
Ordered dithering of a channel value c to n levels: B is the Bayer threshold at the pixel (0 to 1) and a the dithering slider.
Fog: strongest at the top of the frame, gone below 62% of its height; f is the fog slider.

presets.text: Few lines and 64 colours go back to the earliest 3D.
Full wobble with no fog shows the mesh at work.
Turn the display and scan lines off for a clean low-resolution frame.
